Lead story

Ray: Okay, so here's the problem. Density functional theory, which I'll call D F T from here on, is the workhorse calculation behind materials databases and machine learning models. You run it until it's converged, meaning energy changes and leftover errors fall below set thresholds.

Ada: And converged means correct?

Ray: Here's the thing. The authors show those criteria can accept a state where the energy could still go down. Even two independent optimizers agreeing doesn't fix it.

Ada: So what did they actually do?

Ray: They built a descent probe. It starts from the answer a code returns and looks for lower states you can reach from there. They also made a frozen orbital test, called a Janak test, that catches cases where the Hamiltonian doesn't match the energy. Both work with any code, no modification.

Ada: And the result?

Ray: In VASP, a uranium dioxide calculation converged one point four six electron volts above a lower state. Cobalt oxide and iron oxide converged as metals, eight tenths to nine tenths of an electron volt above their insulating states. Then they ran a census of three hundred thirty nine converged Materials Project structures. Fifty seven of them, sixteen point eight percent, showed energy drops above the threshold. Forty nine of those had no initial energy rise bigger than the tolerance.

Ada: Sixteen point eight percent is big. But they recomputed those structures with a modified static protocol. Is that the database being wrong, or their setup?

Ray: Fair question. The summary says the protocol was modified, but it doesn't say how, so I can't split those two apart.

Ada: And does a lower energy mean the real material sits in that state?

Ray: The abstract doesn't claim that. It's about the calculation, not an experiment. My read, and it's interpretation, is that computed magnetic labels are less settled than they look.

Ada: Which matters, because models train on those labels.

Ray: Exactly. If the label is a state that isn't the lowest, the model learns it anyway.

Magnets and materials

Ray: Staying on magnets. Iron one third niobium disulfide is a layered magnet, and the paper reports a surface and bulk split. Photoemission matches A type antiferromagnetism, but neutron scattering and bulk DFT plus U point to stripe order.

Ada: Those can't both be right. Unless the surface is different.

Ray: That's the resolution. Slab calculations show that relaxing an iron terminated surface flips the preference from stripe to A type. The authors caution against assuming photoemission signals reflect the bulk magnetic state.

Ada: Nice, and it's a calculation explaining a measurement.

Ray: Next, neodymium four antimony three, a ferromagnet with an experimental Curie temperature near seventy two kelvin. Monte Carlo simulations built on calculated exchange couplings give about seventy eight. Those calculations include anisotropic exchange and Dzyaloshinskii Moriya interactions.

Ada: Six kelvin off. Good or bad?

Ray: The paper calls it close. It's one material, so I'd treat it as a data point, not a benchmark for the whole method.

Ray: And in monolayer chromium diiodide, Jahn Teller distortion gives opposite sign Kitaev couplings on short and long bonds. A machine learned spin Hamiltonian reproduces the observed proper screw magnetic order.

DFT 'converged' states often aren't ground states, even in Materials Project

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 7/10

The abstract reports that standard convergence criteria can accept magnetic states that are not the lowest in energy. In VASP, a UO2 PBE+U calculation converged 1.46 eV above its ground state, and CoO and FeO converged as metals 0.8-0.9 eV above their insulating states. In a census of 339 Materials Project structures, 57 (16.8%) showed energy drops above threshold, a sign that computed magnetic labels can be less settled than they look.

Fe1/3NbS2 surface and bulk favor different magnetic orders

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 8/10

The abstract reports that ARPES matches A-type antiferromagnetism in Fe1/3NbS2, while neutron scattering and bulk DFT+U point to stripe order. DFT+U slab calculations show that relaxing an iron-terminated surface flips the preferred state to A-type. It is a clear case where the surface and the bulk of one material can host different magnetic orders.

DFT-mapped Heisenberg model plus Monte Carlo reproduces almandine's T_N

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 7/10

The abstract reports that DFT energies were mapped onto a Heisenberg model, then simulated with classical Monte Carlo using a quantum-to-classical spin rescaling. The resulting Néel temperature of about 9.8 K matches specific-heat measurements of almandine, a garnet mineral. It is a full chain from first-principles energies to a finite-temperature prediction for an antiferromagnet.

Nd4Sb3: DFT exchange and Monte Carlo give Tc near 78 K

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports a ferromagnet with an experimental Curie temperature of about 72 K, while Monte Carlo simulations built on calculated exchange couplings give about 78 K. The calculations include anisotropic exchange and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions. It is a useful benchmark for how close computed-exchange predictions land to measured transition temperatures in a rare-earth ferromagnet.

Event cameras beat RGB in low light and fast motion, fusion best

arXiv · event-based vision · 6/10

The abstract reports that the best event-camera detector reached 27.2 AP in low light, against 21.3 AP for an RGB detector, and late fusion of the two reached 33.3 AP. At high speed (above 20 pixels per frame), RGB found 11-19% of medium-sized objects versus 39-60% for an event detector. The data come from a construction site, so applying the results to metal melt pools would be an extrapolation.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Jahn-Teller distortion gives mixed-sign Kitaev exchange in CrI2

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports opposite-sign Kitaev couplings on short and long bonds in monolayer CrI2, a pattern that holds across Hubbard U, functional choice and strain. A machine-learned spin Hamiltonian built with a cluster expansion reproduces the observed proper-screw magnetic order. The result bears on how magnetic exchange and anisotropy vary bond by bond in a two-dimensional magnet.

ML screen finds 249 bipolar anomalous Nernst candidates, tested in Co2TiGe

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports a machine-learning screen for materials with a bipolar anomalous Nernst effect, a transverse voltage produced by heat flow in a magnet. Single-crystal measurements confirmed a sign change near 225 K in Co2TiGe, one of the screened candidates. The work is a screening-to-experiment loop, though it concerns thermoelectrics rather than magnetic anisotropy.

Team cuts heavy rare-earth use in Nd-Fe-B magnets

Phys.org · Materials · 7/10

According to the press text, the team aims to minimize heavy rare earths in neodymium-iron-boron magnets while keeping coercivity at high temperature. The method and results are not in the item, so the claims are unconfirmed. Heavy rare earths such as dysprosium are costly and supply-constrained, which makes this a live research direction.

Frozen MLIP embeddings predict properties they weren't trained on

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports that frozen embeddings from the machine-learned interatomic potentials ORB-v3 and UMA-S beat composition-only descriptors on nine properties across 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Simple nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches the performance of XGBoost. Magnetic properties are not mentioned in the abstract, so it is unclear whether they were among the nine targets.

Nikon SLM Solutions introduces MACHX metal LPBF system

TCT interviews the company about its new MACHX metal laser powder bed fusion system, with the stated focus on scaling and reliability. The item does not describe monitoring features, so whether the machine ships with in-situ sensing is unknown.

Theoretical Physics

Complex-conjugate Ising model: PT breaking occurs before true criticality

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports that finite-size scaling confirms the 2D Ising universality class along the critical line, while the spectrum turns complex at a separate point K_PT below the critical coupling. Correlations stay short-ranged there, so the spectral transition is not a thermodynamic critical point. It is a reminder that a spectral signature does not automatically mark a phase transition.

Imaginary-time Krylov methods cut finite-temperature cost for transverse-field Ising

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports two imaginary-time Krylov methods that need about half as many operator applications as standard finite-temperature Lanczos at N=32, benchmarked against quantum Monte Carlo. The methods work near the quantum critical point of the transverse-field Ising model. Cheaper finite-temperature methods matter because exact calculations become costly as system size grows.

How fast can gravity entangle two masses, and what does noise cost?

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

A proposed test would ask whether gravity is quantum by checking if two small masses placed in superposition become entangled through their mutual gravity. The abstract reports a maximum noiseless entangling rate that falls as the inverse cube of separation, and noise lowers it further to at least the inverse fourth power. Beyond a certain noise level, classical signals can mimic gravity's leading pull, which shows how demanding the experiment is.

A 20-year galaxy survey hints the leading cosmology model is missing something

Quanta Magazine · Physics · 6/10

Quanta reports that the final results of a 20-year galaxy survey do not quite fit the leading theory of cosmology. Only the teaser is available, so the specific tension is unconfirmed. The broad idea is that precise maps of how galaxies cluster test the standard picture of dark matter and dark energy.
